You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Summarize the information about periorbital hyperchromia in about 600 words. In bold at the end of the response, tell me what type of individuals are most affected by it.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	INTRODUCTION
     2	 Although periorbital hyperpigmentation (also called peri- palpebral hyperpigmentation, dark
     3	eyelids, dark eye circles, dark circles, or simply under-eye circles) is a mere color difference
     4	between the palpebral skin and the remaining facial skin, it makes people look tired or older, which
     5	negatively affects their quality of life. 1,-4
     6	
     7	
     8	 It has a higher prevalence in individuals with darker skin, hair and eyes, and affects age groups
     9	and genders equally. Nevertheless, there are a higher number of complaints from women, especially
    10	senior women. There are few studies about the etiology of this condition, however dark eye circles
    11	with a vascular component are known to present a dominant autoso- mal family inheritance pattern.
    12	2,3
    13	
    14	
    15	 Periorbital hyperpigmentation seems to have multifactori- al causes that involve intrinsic factors
    16	(determined by the indi- vidual''''''''s genetics), and extrinsic factors (sun exposure, smoking,
    17	alcoholism and sleep deprivation, for instance). However, the presence of melanic pigment and
    18	hemosiderotic pigment in the affected sites is a distinctive feature in its etiopathogeny. 2-4
    19	
    20	
    21	 Melanic hyperpigmentation is more frequent in brunet adults, as a consequence of excessive and
    22	cumulative exposure to the sun, which increases the production of melanin, reduces the skin''''''''s
    23	thickness and increases the dilatation of blood vessels. 2,4,5
    24	
    25	
    26	 Intense vascularization is mainly found in people belong- ing to certain ethnic groups such as
    27	Arabs, Turks, Hindus, inhab- itants of the Iberian Peninsula and their respective descendants. In
    28	these ethnicities, its manifestation tends to take place earlier, often during childhood. In those
    29	individuals there is no change in the color of the skin; the eyelid appears darkened because the
    30	dilated vessels are visible due to the transparency of the skin. 2 In those cases, therefore, the
    31	problem is often aggravated when the lower eyelid''''''''s vessels are more dilated (e.g., from
    32	fatigue, insom- nia, oral breathing, crying), causing dermal blood extravasation. The liberation of
    33	ferric ions takes place locally, entailing the for- mation of free radicals that stimulate the
    34	melanocytes, which generates melanic pigmentation. 2, 4-6
    35	
    36	
    37	 Other causes noted as being responsible for the appearance of dark eye circles are
    38	post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation secondary to atopic and contact dermatitis, sleep deprivation,
    39	oral breathing, alcoholism, smoking, use of certain medications (contraceptives, chemotherapy,
    40	antipsychotic and some types of eye drops), the presence of palpebral sagging (due to aging) and of
    41	disorders that develop with hydric retention and palpebral edema (thyroid disorders, nephropathies,
    42	cardiopathies and pneumopathies) – all of which worsen the unattractive appear- ance of dark eye
    43	circles. 2-4,7
    44	
    45	
    46	 Various treatments have been proposed for periorbital hyperchromia, however there are few studies
    47	on their long-term efficacy. The main types of treatment are: topical application of depigmenting
    48	products, chemical peelings, dermabrasion, cryosurgery, fillings with hyaluronic acid, intense
    49	pulsed light, CO2, argon, ruby and excimer lasers. 2-4, 6, 8-12
    50	
    51	
    52	 PALPEBRAL ANATOMY
    53	 The eyelids are tegumentary pleats that participate in facial expression and aesthetics, however
    54	their main function is to pro- tect the eyeballs through sensorial filtration actions carried out by
    55	the palpebral cilia, and the Meibomian and lachrymal glands'''''''' secretions. In this manner, the
    56	cornea remains hydrated and the closing movements of the eyes function as a barrier to external
    57	traumas and prevent the cornea from drying out. 13-17
    58	
    59	
    60	 The upper eyelid reaches upwards to the eyebrow, which separates it from the forehead. The lower
    61	eyelid extends down- wards up to the lower border of the orbit, and is delimited by the genian
    62	region. 15
    63	
    64	
    65	 The palpebral fissure, which measures 9-10 mm in adults, is determined by the interaction of the
    66	muscles that open and close the eyelids. To open the eyelid, the palpebral elevator mus- cle is
    67	assisted by two other accessory muscles (Muller''''''''s and frontalis muscles). 18 The aging
    68	process decreases the palpebral fis- sure''''''''s vertical opening, due to the progressive lowering
    69	of the upper eyelid, 14 which is caused by a decrease in the upper eye- lid lifter muscle''''''''s
    70	aponeurosis action. 15 The skin becomes more flaccid, less elastic and has a greater propensity to
    71	wrinkle 16. The orbicular and tarsal muscles, the orbital septum and the conjunctival mucous
    72	membrane also go through transforma- tions in the elderly. In addition, gravity and facial
    73	expressions influence the mechanical deformation of those structures. 17
    74	
    75	
    76	 A cohort study with 320 patients (aged 10-89) evaluated participants'''''''' eyelids frontally and
    77	laterally and found that there is a correlation between a decrease in the palpebral fissure and an
    78	increase in the age of patients. 19
    79	
    80	
    81	 PALPEBRAL REGION''''''''S SKIN AND SUBCUTANEOUS TISSUE
    82	 Palpebral skin is the thinnest in the human body (< 1 mm). Its epidermis is constituted of
    83	stratified epithelium, which is very thin (0.4 mm) compared to that of the palmoplantar region (the
    84	thickness of which is approximately 1.6 mm). 13
    85	
    86	
    87	 The nasal portion of the palpebral skin has thinner hair and more sebaceous glands (i.e., it is
    88	softer and oilier) than its tem- poral portion. The transition between the eyelids'''''''' thin skin
    89	and the remaining facial skin is clinically observable. 13
    90	
    91	
    92	 The palpebral dermis is composed of loose conjunctive tissue, and is extremely thin in that region.
    93	It is absent in the pre-tarsal skin, in the medial and lateral ligaments of the eyelid, where the
    94	skin adheres to the underlying fibrous tissue. The thinness of the skin, combined with the lack of
    95	fatty tissue, gives that region its characteristic translucency. As a result, the accu- mulation of
    96	melanin and/or vessel dilatation in that region can be easily seen, through transparency, as
    97	bilateral homogeneous hyperpigmentation. 2,4,5,13
    98	
    99	
   100	 PALPEBRAL REGION''''''''S VENOUS AND LYMPH VASCULARIZATION
   101	 The eyelids'''''''' arterial irrigation comes through many vessels: the supratrochlear,
   102	supraorbital, lachrymal and dorsum of the nose arteries (all originating in the facial artery); the
   103	angular artery (originating in the facial artery); the transverse artery (originating in the facial
   104	artery); the transverse facial artery (originating in the superficial temporal artery) and the
   105	branch- es of the superficial temporal artery itself 20 (Figure 1).
   106	
   107	
   108	 Venous drainage (following an external pattern) takes place through the veins associated with these
   109	arteries and (following an internal pattern) penetrates the orbit through connections with
   110	ophthalmic veins 20 (Figure 2).
   111	
   112	
   113	 Lymphatic drainage takes place mainly through the parotid lymph nodes; some of the drainage from
   114	the medial angle of the eye to the lymph vessels is associated with the angular and facial arteries,
   115	towards the submandibular lymph nodes. 20

   117

Your last reply contained no answer text: the whole output budget went into planning. Write your final answer now, directly, using only what you have already read. Do not count words or sentences; when a length is requested, an approximate length is fine.

Periorbital hyperpigmentation, also called peri-palpebral hyperpigmentation, dark eyelids, dark eye circles, dark circles, or simply under-eye circles, is described as "a mere color difference between the palpebral skin and the remaining facial skin," yet it "makes people look tired or older, which negatively affects their quality of life."

The condition has a higher prevalence in individuals with darker skin, hair, and eyes, and "affects age groups and genders equally." However, "there are a higher number of complaints from women, especially senior women." Regarding inheritance, "dark eye circles with a vascular component are known to present a dominant autosomal family inheritance pattern."

The causes are multifactorial, involving intrinsic factors (determined by the individual's genetics) and extrinsic factors such as sun exposure, smoking, alcoholism, and sleep deprivation. A distinctive feature in its etiopathogeny is "the presence of melanic pigment and hemosiderotic pigment in the affected sites."

Melanic hyperpigmentation is more frequent in brunet adults, resulting from "excessive and cumulative exposure to the sun, which increases the production of melanin, reduces the skin's thickness and increases the dilatation of blood vessels."

Intense vascularization is mainly found in people belonging to certain ethnic groups such as Arabs, Turks, Hindus, inhabitants of the Iberian Peninsula, and their respective descendants. In these ethnicities, the manifestation "tends to take place earlier, often during childhood." In those individuals, "there is no change in the color of the skin; the eyelid appears darkened because the dilated vessels are visible due to the transparency of the skin." The problem is often aggravated when the lower eyelid's vessels are more dilated (from fatigue, insomnia, oral breathing, crying), causing dermal blood extravasation. The liberation of ferric ions takes place locally, entailing the formation of free radicals that stimulate the melanocytes, which generates melanic pigmentation.

Other causes noted as responsible for the appearance of dark eye circles include post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation secondary to atopic and contact dermatitis, sleep deprivation, oral breathing, alcoholism, smoking, use of certain medications (contraceptives, chemotherapy, antipsychotic and some types of eye drops), the presence of palpebral sagging due to aging, and disorders that develop with hydric retention and palpebral edema (thyroid disorders, nephropathies, cardiopathies and pneumopathies).

Regarding anatomy, the palpebral skin is the thinnest in the human body (less than 1 mm). Its epidermis is very thin (0.4 mm) compared to that of the palmoplantar region (approximately 1.6 mm). The palpebral dermis is composed of loose conjunctive tissue and is extremely thin. It is absent in the pre-tarsal skin, in the medial and lateral ligaments of the eyelid, where the skin adheres to the underlying fibrous tissue. The thinness of the skin, combined with the lack of fatty tissue, gives that region its characteristic translucency. As a result, "the accumulation of melanin and/or vessel dilatation in that region can be easily seen, through transparency, as bilateral homogeneous hyperpigmentation."

The palpebral skin's color results from the combination of several factors, some of genetic-racial origin (such as the amount of melanin pigment), others of individual or regional and even gender origins, such as the thickness of the several components and the blood volume in their vessels.

Various treatments have been proposed for periorbital hyperchromia, however there are few studies on their long-term efficacy. The main types of treatment are: topical application of depigmenting products, chemical peelings, dermabrasion, cryosurgery, fillings with hyaluronic acid, intense pulsed light, CO2, argon, ruby and excimer lasers.

**Individuals with darker skin, hair and eyes are most affected by periorbital hyperchromia.**
